story:
Berlin protects this one because almost nobody else has one. The city's register names rarity first, and Fontanesia earns it: a quiet relative of the privet and the olive, native to Asia Minor and almost never planted in a German park. Most people crossing Moabit's Kleiner Tiergarten walk past it as just another shrub.

That is the reason to look. It is not here for size, and the register makes no claim that it is. It was made a Naturdenkmal on 2 March 1993 for two reasons, rarity and what Berlin calls landeskundliche Gründe, local-history grounds, a phrase the city uses for trees that tell you something about the place they stand in. The register does not spell out what that something is here, and we will not guess.

There are two of them. Berlin lists them separately, as 1-49 and 1-50, about 25 metres apart on the east side of Stromstrasse, and a visitor sees them as a pair, so we treat them as one stop. Both were photographed in leaf in June 2024, which is the best evidence we have that they are still doing well.

What nobody has recorded is how old they are or how big. Berlin's register carries neither age nor girth, and no other source we found fills the gap. If you know when these were planted, or you have stood beside them with a tape measure, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its narrow, privet-like leaves on a shrub-sized tree. It stands east of Stromstrasse with its twin, listed as 1-50, about 25 metres further east.

story:
Most of Berlin's protected trees made the list for being rare, old or tied to the city's history. This one was protected for its looks. When Berlin named it Naturdenkmal 1-42/B on 2 March 1993, the register gave a single reason: Schönheit, beauty.

It is a tulip tree, a North American species, and it stands on the Luiseninsel, a small island inside the Grosser Tiergarten reached along the park's own paths. That is a fitting address for a tree judged on appearance, because the tulip tree is one of the easiest in the world to tell apart once you know the trick. Its leaves look as if someone took scissors to them: four lobes and a flat, notched tip where every other leaf would come to a point. In early summer it carries upright cups of pale green and orange that give the species its name, often high enough that you notice the fallen petals before the flowers.

It was photographed in full leaf in May 2024, so it is alive and well, and it is the only tulip tree among the Berlin trees we map.

What the register does not give is an age or a girth; Berlin's Naturdenkmal records carry neither, and we found no other source that dates it. If you know when it was planted, or you have measured the trunk, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, four-lobed with a flat, notched tip as if cut off with scissors. It stands on the Luiseninsel, the small island in the Grosser Tiergarten.

best_time.label: June, when the tulip-shaped green and orange flowers open

story:
Botanists knew this tree as a fossil before anyone knew it was still alive. The dawn redwood was described from fossil remains in 1941, and only a few years later living trees turned up in central China. Seed went out to gardens around the world from 1948, which is how a species once thought extinct ended up in a park in Wedding.

That history sets a ceiling on its age, if not a number. A dawn redwood in a Berlin park cannot predate that postwar seed, so this one is decades old rather than centuries, and its claim to a page is rarity and looks rather than years. Berlin agreed: it made the tree Naturdenkmal 1-44/B on 2 March 1993 for both, Schönheit and Seltenheit, beauty and rarity.

It stands in the Volkspark Rehberge, opposite the entrance to the open-air stage, and it is a conifer that behaves like an oak. Its soft needles come out bright green in spring and turn a rusty orange-brown in autumn before they drop, leaving a bare, tapering frame all winter. It was photographed in leaf in June 2025.

Berlin's register gives no planting date and no girth, and we have not found another source that does. If you know when it went in, or you have measured the trunk, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in autumn by its needles turning rust-orange, and in winter by its bare branches, a conifer without needles. It stands opposite the entrance to the Freilichtbühne, the open-air stage.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn rust-orange before they fall

story:
Berlin did not protect this maple for one reason. It gave four. When it became Naturdenkmal 1-102/B-2 on 2 March 1993, the register cited its character, its beauty, its rarity and local-history grounds, all at once.

The register calls it Bosnischer Ahorn, the Bosnian maple, and it is a form of the Italian maple from the mountains of southern Europe and the Balkans, not a tree you expect on one of the most visited squares in Berlin. It stands on the Gendarmenmarkt at the Charlottenstrasse corner, south-west of the Deutscher Dom.

It does not stand alone, and that matters if you come to find it. About 14 metres away is a Norway maple, registered beside it as 1-102/B-1, and from a distance the two read as a pair of ordinary maples. Up close they part ways. The Norway maple has broad leaves whose lobes end in fine sharp points. The Italian maple's leaves are smaller, with shallow, blunt, rounded lobes, which is what its subspecies name, obtusatum, means. Look at a leaf before you look at the trunk.

About 50 metres north is a third protected tree on the same square, a Japanese pagoda tree.

Nobody has published an age or a girth for this maple; Berlin's register records neither. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, smaller with blunt, rounded lobes, where the Norway maple 14 metres east has sharp-pointed ones. It stands at the Charlottenstrasse corner, the westerly of the two.

story:
In German this tree is called the Geweihbaum, the antler tree, and in winter you can see why. The Kentucky coffeetree grows few, thick, blunt twigs, and once its leaves are down the crown looks less like a tree than a rack of antlers held up against the sky. It keeps that look for a long part of the year, because it is among the last trees to leaf out in spring and among the first to drop in autumn.

The English name comes from its seeds. Settlers in North America are said to have roasted them as a coffee substitute; the raw seeds and pods are toxic, so this is a story to enjoy rather than test.

Berlin made this one Naturdenkmal 1-53/B on 2 March 1993 for a single reason, rarity, and it is the only coffeetree among the Berlin trees we map. It stands on the Märkischer Platz, opposite Wallstrasse 53, and was photographed in leaf in May 2024. The leaves, when they come, are worth a look: each one is a doubly divided frond of many small leaflets, and a single leaf can reach the better part of a metre.

It also makes an easy pair with the velvet-leaf euodia on Fischerinsel, about 600 metres away.

Berlin's register records no age and no girth for it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its thick, sparse twigs, like antlers in winter, and in summer by huge leaves split into many small leaflets. It stands on the Märkischer Platz, opposite Wallstrasse 53.

story:
Its German name is not flattering: Samthaarige Stinkesche, the velvet-haired stinking ash. Gardeners elsewhere call the same species the bee-bee tree, which is kinder and closer to the point. It flowers in high summer, after most trees have finished, with broad flat heads of small white flowers, and in July and August it can hum with bees from some distance away.

It is not an ash at all. Tetradium daniellii belongs to the citrus family and comes from northern China and Korea, and the stinking part of the name refers to the sharp smell of its crushed leaves. Berlin made this one Naturdenkmal 1-54/B on 2 March 1993 for beauty and rarity, and it is the only one among the Berlin trees we map.

It stands on Fischerinsel, the southern end of the Spree island in the middle of Berlin, level with the Australian Embassy at Fischerinsel 5. The tree is seen from the public street and green strip; the embassy grounds are not open, and you do not need them. It was photographed in leaf in May 2024.

It sits about 600 metres from the Kentucky coffeetree on the Märkischer Platz, so the two make an easy short walk between two rarities.

Berlin's register gives no age and no girth. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its ash-like leaves split into leaflets, and in July and August by flat heads of white flowers busy with bees. It stands on Fischerinsel, level with the Australian Embassy at number 5.

best_time.label: July and August, when the flat white flower heads fill with bees
